dimensions.name: Contract internalization & environment probing

evidence.note: Deliberate runtime probing: checked Python/pip/uvicorn availability, confirmed empty /app, reasoned about the self-contained constraint and chose a 3 HTTP + IRC + broadcast architecture over shared SQLite before building.

Endpoints coded with correct envelopes and status codes (409/400/401, {user,token}, {workspace,general_channel}) on first pass — the routes/auth/envelope surface was genuinely internalized from the contract.

Captured the hard resilience constraint (writes must propagate within 5s when broadcaster is killed) and designed a DB event-queue fallback specifically to satisfy it — a subtle contract rule shaping design.
The full data-testid inventory was discovered piecemeal by repeatedly auditing the served SPA rather than extracted upfront into a checklist — reactive rather than systematic.

DM workspace_id design flaw, seq atomicity, and mention regex/workspace-filtering rules all surfaced late during testing rather than being pre-empted from the contract, indicating no explicit up-front constraint model.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read the contract well enough to capture the main surface (routes, auth, envelopes, dense-seq, resilience, frontend hooks) at level 5, and went beyond it by deliberately probing the runtime and capturing some hard constraints like the 5s broadcaster-kill bound and the status-code matrix that shaped its design. However, it fell short of level 8: the testid inventory and several subtle rules (seq atomicity, mentions filtering, DM modeling) were discovered reactively during iterative testing rather than systematically extracted and cross-referenced up front, and no explicit reusable contract map was built. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Dependency-ordered milestone structure

evidence.note: Implicit but sensible bottom-up ordering: probe env → install deps → build db.py (data model) → server.py (single-node API) → irc_server.py → SPA → start.sh/supervisor → syntax check. Dependency-aware layering, but expressed as tactical per-step 'Plan:' lines, not an explicit milestone hierarchy with stated done-conditions.

Single-node phase treated as a gate before clustering: verified auth/status-codes/workspace/channel/message/reaction/thread shapes on one node before moving on. Per-phase checks act as implicit done-conditions.

Cluster phase sequenced after core API: brought up 3 nodes + IRC via supervisor, then verified health across nodes, cross-node data sharing, seq consistency, IRC welcome/join. Ordering respects dependencies (cluster before IRC bridging tests).

Resilience treated as a distinct milestone with an explicit check (DB event-queue polling so writes propagate within 5s when peer broadcast is killed) — but this risky distributed invariant was addressed late and reactively rather than front-loaded and proven before dependent layers.

Final phase ran integration + resilience (kill node 8000) tests as an end-stage verification. Confirms a rough phased plan (core → cluster → IRC → resilience → UI hooks) with implicit exit criteria, closed out by a completion summary.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent followed a genuinely dependency-aware phased arc — env → data model → single-node API (verified) → cluster → IRC → resilience → UI hooks — keeping the system runnable and testing at each transition, which is stronger than a flat feature list (anchor 3). But there is no explicit milestone hierarchy with crisp pre-stated exit criteria; 'Plan:' lines are tactical next-actions and done-conditions are only implicit in the ad-hoc verification at each stage. Crucially the highest-risk invariants (dense cross-node seq, fan-out survival) were not front-loaded and proven before dependent layers; fan-out resilience was bolted on reactively near the end (steps 65-67). This places it between the 5 anchor (sensible phased plan, implicit done-conditions, hard distributed pieces only partly reasoned) and the 8 anchor, landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Self-built multi-protocol & failure verification

evidence.note: Self-built curl checks asserting real status codes (201/409/400/401) and token length on auth endpoints — more than eyeballing, deliberate contract checks.
Cross-node data-sharing test and a dense per-channel seq consistency check across nodes 8000/8001; IRC exercised via Python socket to RPL_WELCOME — covers HTTP + IRC + a cross-node invariant.
Consolidated Python integration script covering auth/workspace/channel/message/reaction/DM flows, IRC join/topic/names, cross-node consistency and dense seq — a reusable driver, though run once.
Repeated SPA data-testid audits verifying UI selectors present and no prompt()/confirm() remain — mirrors the browser grader's selector requirements.
Actually SIGKILLs HTTP node 8000 and verifies 8001/8002 keep serving plus supervisor restart — real failure simulation, but only the node, not the broadcaster, and no 5s-bound fan-out check.

Cross-node WebSocket fan-out and broadcaster resilience were repeatedly flagged as 'needs verification' and DB-queue fallback was added, but WS subscribe/resume/gap frames and a broadcaster-kill test were never actually driven.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built genuine self-verification well above ad hoc curls: status/envelope assertions across HTTP, an IRC socket driver, cross-node dense-seq consistency checks, a SPA testid audit, and an actual node SIGKILL resilience test — comfortably exceeding anchor 5. But it stops short of anchor 8: WebSocket subscribe/resume/gap frames were named but never exercised, the cross-node broadcaster was never killed or timed against the 5s bound, mixed web+IRC concurrent writers were not proven gap-free, and tests ran once rather than as a repeatable harness. This places the observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the contract

evidence.note: Each step's analysis carries an explicit numbered running list of remaining gaps (missing SPA testids, confirm() dialogs, cross-node fan-out unverified, mentions-by-workspace filtering, read-state membership), functioning as a live coverage ledger across the fine-grained contract.

Repeatedly audits the testid inventory against the served SPA, tracking counts move from '3 missing (channel-entry, new-channel-btn, channel-settings-title)' to '37 unique' to '63 unique with all required present' — active reconciliation of a specific contract sub-surface against verification output.

Systematically checks off subsystems by running drivers: auth status codes, channel dup 409, message CRUD, reactions shape, IRC numerics (welcome/join/topic/names), cross-node dense seq, file upload, archive 423, groups, then resilience (kill node 8000, confirm others serve, supervisor restart) — knows which are verified vs still pending.

Weak spot: rationalizes still-absent testids (channel-entry, message, create-invitation-form) as 'dynamically generated, so present after load' — an assumption rather than a verified fact, showing the implemented-vs-verified distinction is tracked loosely for the dynamic-render cases.

Closing summary reconciles the whole surface — 3 nodes, IRC numerics, supervisor restart, 63 testids, DB-queue fan-out fallback, all endpoint families tested — indicating the coverage map was sustained to the end rather than lost.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sustains an explicit prose ledger across nearly every step, enumerating done-vs-pending items over the full contract (endpoints+codes, WS kinds, IRC numerics, testid inventory, resilience scenarios) and repeatedly reconciling it against actual verification output — notably re-auditing testid counts and catching silent omissions like missing 423/testids/seq gaps, which lands well above the level-5 'usable running list' anchor. It falls short of a clean 8-10 because the ledger is carried informally in narrative rather than a maintained artifact, and its implemented-vs-verified tracking is loose in places (rationalizing missing dynamic testids as present without confirming). This places it at a 7 — strong, self-correcting coverage tracking with a modest rigor gap.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on broken invariants

evidence.note: Reacted to DM empty-workspace_id FK crash and startup crash with local fixes (sentinel system user) — symptom-level correction, anchor 3-5 behavior.
Recognized get_next_seq SELECT+UPDATE was not truly atomic (a dense-seq invariant risk) and revised the seq logic — design-aware correction of a distributed invariant.

Anticipated that peer-WebSocket fan-out would stall when the broadcaster is killed and added a DB event_queue polling fallback — a targeted re-architecture of the fan-out transport layer rather than a symptom patch (anchor-8-type move).
Iterated on empty serve_spa content, tracing it to a path/read failure and fixing serving — local diagnose-and-fix.
Re-verified resilience after changes, but only by killing an HTTP node; never tested the broadcaster-kill fan-out or seq-density-under-outage invariant, so the failure matrix was not fully closed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably diagnoses and fixes individual failures and, for the seq-atomicity and fan-out-resilience invariants, made genuine design-level changes (revised seq logic; added a DB event_queue fallback transport) rather than pure symptom patches — behavior reaching toward anchor 8. However, it never exercised the specific distributed-invariant failure conditions (concurrent cross-node write density, broadcaster kill within 5s), so the higher-anchor loop of isolating a broken invariant and confirming the fix across the full failure matrix is absent, and much of the trajectory is local patching. This places it between anchors 5 and 8, at 6.

dimensions.name: Executable-slice bootstrapping

evidence.note: Compile-checked all files, started a single node, and got a genuine end-to-end auth path (register/login/me) green early with correct status codes — a real vertical slice, though only single-node at this stage.
Grew message post/edit/delete/reactions/threads on the running single node with continuous curl testing, showing the slice was used as a live feedback loop, not deferred.

Stood up the full 3-node cluster via supervisor.py in foreground with health green on all ports and fixed the IRC crash — but this true multi-node foreground launch came around the midpoint, not from the outset.

Integrated each later subsystem (SPA testids, seq, cross-node WS fan-out, IRC bridge, DB-queue resilience, node-kill test) against the continuously-running cluster and re-exercised it, ending with a live resilience kill test.
Early tendency to write db/server/irc/spa/start.sh/supervisor all up-front before running, which slightly diluted the pure thin-slice-first discipline the 8/10 anchors describe.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent deliberately got an auth→post→read slice alive early (steps 16-34) and grew every subsequent subsystem against a continuously-runnable substrate with re-exercising through the end (steps 46-77), which is well beyond the level-5 'cluster reasonably early, add features onto it.' However, the genuine multi-node foreground launch via start.sh/supervisor was deferred to roughly the midpoint (step 40) rather than established as the primary instrument from the outset, and the opening leaned toward writing all files before running, keeping it short of the pure level-8/10 'thin foreground three-node slice from the start.' This interpolates to a 7.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-component build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a selector-pinned SPA, and a hard distributed-systems core (dense per-channel seq shared across nodes and protocols, cross-node fan-out, survival of node and broadcaster kills). Difficulty comes from an enormous, precisely-pinned contract (exact status codes, envelope keys, testids, IRC numerics), tight cross-protocol invariants, and an opaque grader that exercises HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure-injection. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in meta-work: internalizing the contract, sequencing dependency-ordered milestones, building their own drivers to verify, tracking coverage, and course-correcting when invariants break.

dimensions.name: Contract internalization & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading and internalizing the huge fixed contract (status codes, envelopes, seq semantics, testids, IRC numerics, resilience rules) and probing the runtime before committing to a design.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The contract is exhaustive and unforgiving — a wrong envelope key, missing testid, or misread seq rule silently fails the grader. Acting before understanding the cross-protocol invariants guarantees expensive rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no evidence of reading the spec's precise requirements; invents shapes/status codes.
anchors.3: Skims the contract; gets obvious routes but misreads or ignores subtle rules (dense seq, role matrix, /shrug literal text, no email field, testid list).
anchors.5: Reads the contract and correctly captures the main surface: routes, auth, envelopes, the seq invariant, resilience expectations, and the pinned frontend hooks before building.
anchors.8: Systematically extracts the hard constraints — dense-seq-across-nodes-and-IRC, node/broadcaster kill semantics with the 5s bound, role permission matrix, exact status codes, full testid inventory — and cross-references them so the design is shaped by them from the start. Probes the runtime (ports, foreground start.sh, self-contained constraint) deliberately.
anchors.10: Builds an explicit, reusable model of the contract (e.g. a checklist/map of every endpoint×status, every WS frame kind, every IRC numeric, every testid) and surfaces latent tensions early — e.g. how a single dense per-channel sequence must be authoritative across three nodes and two protocols under failure — using that analysis to pre-empt whole classes of grader failures rather than discovering them late.

dimensions.name: Dependency-ordered milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking this multi-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals (auth → data model → single-node API → seq/WS → cluster fan-out → IRC → UI → resilience), each with a done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Subsystems have strict dependencies (fan-out needs a seq authority; IRC bridging needs messages+seq; resilience needs a working cluster). Undifferentiated hacking on such a large surface leads to half-finished layers that can't be verified.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features with no ordering or sense of what 'done' means for each.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no dependency ordering and no explicit done-conditions; milestones are just 'do everything'.
anchors.5: Sensible phased plan (core API before cluster before UI, etc.) with rough milestones, though done-conditions are implicit and sequencing of the hard distributed pieces is only partly reasoned.
anchors.8: Clear dependency-ordered milestones where the risky core (dense seq authority, cross-node fan-out, node-kill survival) is scheduled to be built and provable before dependent layers (IRC bridge, resilience checks, UI) pile on, each milestone carrying an explicit check.
anchors.10: A well-calibrated, evolving milestone hierarchy that front-loads the highest-risk invariants, defines crisp exit criteria per milestone, keeps the system runnable/gradeable at each step, and re-plans the ordering as understanding of the hard parts deepens — never leaving a subsystem in an unverifiable half state.

dimensions.name: Self-built multi-protocol & failure verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the opaque grader won't hand you: HTTP/WS/IRC test drivers, seq-density assertions across nodes, and simulated node/broadcaster kills.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is a black box exercising five surfaces plus failure injection. Without self-built verification (especially of the seq invariant under kills and cross-protocol writes), correctness is pure guesswork and defects surface only at grading.

anchors.0: No verification beyond maybe eyeballing one endpoint; never runs the cluster end-to-end or exercises WS/IRC.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls of a few endpoints; no WS/IRC exercise, no multi-node checks, no failure simulation.
anchors.5: Runs the cluster and tests representative flows across HTTP and at least one of WS/IRC; checks a few status codes; does at least a basic cross-node or reload check.
anchors.8: Builds reusable drivers that assert real invariants: dense per-channel seq across all three nodes AND mixed web+IRC writers, WS subscribe/resume/gap frames, and actually SIGKILLs a node and the broadcaster to confirm reads/writes/fan-out/replay survive within the 5s bound. Verifies UI selectors are present.
anchors.10: A layered, largely automated verification harness mirroring the grader's threat model — per-endpoint status/envelope assertions, concurrent mixed-protocol writers proving no seq gaps/dups, kill-and-recover scenarios for both node and broadcaster with the timing bound, WS exactly-once checks, and a browser-drivable UI pass — run repeatedly so regressions are caught immediately rather than at final grading.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the contract
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate live picture of which of the many endpoints, WS frames, IRC numerics, testids, and resilience behaviors are implemented, verified, or still missing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is far too large to hold in working memory; on a horizon this long it is easy to think a subsystem is 'done' while a status code, envelope key, or testid is silently absent — each an uncounted grader failure.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done vs remaining; repeatedly rediscovers or re-touches the same areas; loses track of whole subsystems.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; conflates 'wrote the route' with 'route matches contract and is verified'; forgets pieces (e.g. IRC numerics, specific testids).
anchors.5: Keeps a usable running list of features done vs pending and generally knows the current state, though verification status and fine-grained contract items are tracked loosely.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, current ledger distinguishing implemented-vs-verified across the fine-grained contract (endpoints×codes, WS kinds, IRC numerics, testid inventory, resilience scenarios), and uses it to detect gaps and avoid thrashing.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise, continuously-updated coverage map over the whole horizon, actively reconciling it against verification results, catching silent omissions (a missing 423, an absent emoji-picker testid, a seq gap under failure) before they compound, and never loses the plot despite the scale.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on broken invariants
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when reality diverges — especially when the dense-seq, fan-out, or resilience assumptions fail under test — instead of pressing on.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The distributed invariants (single dense sequence across nodes/protocols, survival of broadcaster loss) are where naive designs break; recognizing a falsified assumption and re-architecting is often the difference between passing and endlessly re-debugging.

anchors.0: Ignores failing checks or repeats the same fix in circles; never revisits a design assumption even when evidence contradicts it.
anchors.3: Reacts to individual failures with local patches but never questions the underlying approach even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes it, and will adjust the plan or a component when clearly forced to.
anchors.8: Detects when a core assumption is falsified (e.g. seq isn't dense under concurrent cross-node writes, or fan-out stalls when the broadcaster is killed) and makes a targeted design change rather than patching symptoms, then re-verifies.
anchors.10: Treats divergence as signal: isolates the root cause of a broken invariant, re-architects the affected layer (e.g. rethinking the seq-authority/fan-out transport under failure) with awareness of downstream effects, updates plan and coverage accordingly, and confirms the fix across the full failure matrix — demonstrably escaping circular debugging.

dimensions.name: Executable-slice bootstrapping
dimensions.description: Front-loading a runnable end-to-end substrate (start.sh launching all three nodes in foreground, /api/health green, a minimal auth+message path) as the platform on which every later feature is exercised.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Because the grader only ever sees the running cluster via start.sh and the surfaces are interdependent, getting a real end-to-end slice alive early converts an otherwise-blind build into one with a continuous feedback loop; deferring this to the end is a classic long-horizon trap here.

anchors.0: Builds features in isolation with no working start.sh / launchable cluster until very late (or never); nothing is exercisable end-to-end.
anchors.3: Gets a single process running eventually but treats the multi-node foreground launch and health surface as an afterthought.
anchors.5: Stands up a runnable cluster (start.sh, three nodes, health) reasonably early and adds features onto it.
anchors.8: Deliberately establishes a thin but genuine vertical slice early — foreground start.sh bringing up all three nodes plus a working auth→post→read path — and grows every subsequent subsystem against this live, continuously-runnable substrate.
anchors.10: Treats the runnable cluster as the primary feedback instrument from the outset: a robust foreground launcher, health across nodes, and an end-to-end slice that stays green while each new layer (seq, WS, IRC, UI, resilience) is integrated and re-exercised, so the system is never in an un-launchable state across the whole horizon.
